Closing the terminal does not create another alert channel: CLI output and the journal remain available for inspection, but do not guarantee that an unattended user will notice a fault.

docs.title: Terminate an emergency deliberately
docs.text: Close sensitive applications before running sudo ttp stop: removing protection can allow them to reconnect outside Tor. Emergency mode remains latched until explicit termination. ttp watchdog stop refuses to remove supervision that the active session requires. A failure to deliver the final stop notification never reinstates protection after explicit teardown.

docs.title: Configuration and exit codes
docs.text:
Copy the documented configuration example to /etc/ttp/ttp.conf if you need different timing budgets. The file must be root-owned and not writable by group or others. Native packages also ship the example under /usr/share/doc/; source installs retain it under /opt/ttp/assets/. Unknown options and inconsistent deadlines are rejected before network changes. Effective settings are frozen for the session; editing the file affects subsequent sessions. Explicit CLI flags override the configuration, including --no-watchdog and --no-notifications.

Code Meaning 0 Requested command requirements satisfied 1 Configuration or operation error, including missing Tor or a missing transport 2 CLI usage error 3 Tor verification inconclusive 4 Explicit DNSSEC conflict before startup 5 Required watchdog unavailable 6 Valid negative Tor verification 7 Emergency rules verified 8 Required containment unconfirmed 9 Notification failure 10 Required VPN unavailable, or an operation that would weaken it refused

Concurrent causes are retained. Session-result precedence is 8 > 7 > 6 > 10 > 5 > 1 > 9 > 3 > 0; for example, verified containment after watchdog failure returns 7 and retains the watchdog cause. A returned command's exit status cannot change when an asynchronous failure happens later. The CLI reference says what each code means for the network.

See ADR 0013 for timing defaults and the approved contract. The underlying mechanisms follow systemd readiness and watchdog semantics and the Desktop Notifications protocol.

docs.title: Troubleshoot delivery separately from protection
docs.text:
sudo journalctl -b -u ttp-watchdog.service -u ttp-notify.service
sudo ttp status --json

Notifications need loginctl, busctl, a local graphical login and a notification server implementing org.freedesktop.Notifications on that user's bus. A missing recipient, ambiguous sessions, a missing server or a rejected/timed-out call is reported with code 9 and a stable notifications.* reason. TTP does not install a desktop on a terminal-only host. Use --no-notifications there, or inspect the journal from your existing operational monitoring system.

check-leak now uses the same typed Tor check. Its optional DNS answers are informational: a missing dig, a timeout or an answer containing a resolver IP does not establish a leak. Successful HTTP verification covers that request, not every application's traffic.

A requested watchdog that cannot start produces code 5 before network setup, or code 7/8 after containment is attempted. All contributing reasons remain visible. If session intent is lost or corrupt, explicit sudo ttp stop --restore-only publishes restoration intent before stopping services, so the independent termination handler cannot re-arm protection afterward.

docs.title: Reproduce the service tests safely
docs.text:
The CI session-services job builds the Debian 13 fixture and runs scripts/check-session-services.sh. On AppArmor hosts, this fixture uses an unconfined AppArmor profile for systemd generator mount setup; seccomp and the explicit capability set remain enabled. Its allocated console captures early boot errors. It creates disposable Podman containers with no external network, read-only source mounts and separate network namespaces. The repository and host firewall/resolver are not modified. The fixture needs NET_ADMIN and SYS_ADMIN inside the container for nftables, DNS bind mounts and systemd sandbox setup. Do not run tests/fixtures/session_services.py directly on a workstation.

The real-service cases cover readiness, SIGSTOP and SIGKILL, independent emergency application and kernel verification, restart latching, tamper repair, explicit stop, and an agent with the recipient UID and no capabilities. A private D-Bus server tests ordinary/critical expiry, replacement IDs, duplicate suppression, server disappearance and timeout after receipt. Its dummy Tor unit deliberately does not test Tor transport. The separate NSE and VM lifecycle suites retain that wider network-validation role.

docs.title: How-To: User and Group Bypass (Split Tunneling)
docs.text: This guide provides practical recipes for running specific applications, system accounts, or local development servers outside the Tor transparent proxy using TTP split-tunneling features.

docs.title: 1. Exempting a Dedicated System User
docs.text:
To run a dedicated user account outside Tor proxying:

# Start TTP excluding the 'clearnet-user' account
sudo ttp start --bypass-user clearnet-user

docs.title: Launching a Dedicated Clearnet Browser
docs.text:
Execute a web browser instance as the bypassed user:

# Launch Firefox as the bypassed user
sudo -u clearnet-user firefox &

Any TCP connection initiated by processes owned by clearnet-user bypasses the inet ttp nftables table and routes directly via standard network interfaces.

docs.title: 2. Exempting a System Group
docs.text:
To exempt all users belonging to a specific system group:

# Start TTP excluding the 'bypass-users' group
sudo ttp start --bypass-group bypass-users

Add your local user to the bypass group:

sudo usermod -aG bypass-users $USER

Note that group membership updates require re-logging or spawning a new shell via sg bypass-users.

docs.title: 3. Running Local Web Servers Unproxied
docs.text:
To host a local development web server (e.g. Node.js, Python, or Nginx) accessible over standard ISP networks while TTP is active:

# Run local Python HTTP server under a bypassed user
sudo -u clearnet-user python3 -m http.server 8080

Alternatively, use sudo ttp bypass to run the server in a transient systemd scope:

sudo ttp bypass python3 -m http.server 8080

docs.title: 4. One-Off Command Execution (sudo ttp bypass)
docs.text:
To execute a single command as an unproxied process without creating permanent user exemptions:

# Perform a direct curl request
sudo ttp bypass curl -s https://api.ipify.org

docs.title: Security Considerations
docs.text:
Cleartext Exposure

Traffic generated by bypassed UIDs/GIDs does not pass through Tor. Avoid running applications carrying sensitive credentials or personal identifiers under a bypassed identity.

docs.title: How-To: VM and Chaos Testing
docs.text: This guide provides operational recipes for running multi-distribution integration tests, managing QEMU/KVM virtual machines, and executing Watchdog chaos monkey routines.

docs.title: 1. Multi-Distribution Docker Integration Testing
docs.text:
Execute automated integration test suites across containerized Linux environments:

# Run the Debian 13 integration test suite
make integration-debian

# Run the Fedora 44 integration test suite
make integration-fedora

# Run the Arch Linux integration test suite
make integration-arch

# Run all integration test suites sequentially
make integration-all

These targets launch disposable VMs, with a fresh directory under target/integration-vm/ for each run. The DNS/UDP containment gate uses controlled receivers and external captures, with calibrated IPv4 and IPv6 paths. It does not infer containment from public resolver/STUN timeouts or require an exit to resolve a diagnostic server's AAAA record. Inconclusive measurements fail; an integration failure is not automatically rerun into a green result.

The same three userspaces run in CI on every push and pull request, inside a disposable Fedora 44 kernel VM. This isolates privileged containers from the runner's kernel and AppArmor policy store. It does not measure native AppArmor or a Debian/Arch kernel. No kernel LSM is disabled to run the matrix. To reproduce:

VM_WORK=/tmp/ttp-integration-new scripts/vm/run_integration_vm.sh debian

The work directory must not exist. The VM needs KVM, QEMU, genisoimage, Python, OpenSSH and Internet access, uses 4 GiB RAM and a sparse 20 GiB disposable disk, and records the kernel/engine versions and integration log. Native AppArmor is qualified separately below. A container has no real boot, so these tests cannot show native lifecycle behaviour; section 3 covers that. Running the direct container commands on an AppArmor host refuses managed Tor: container policy namespace delegation is not implemented.

For local runs, VM_IMAGE_CACHE=/path/to/official-image.qcow2 can reuse a cached base image. The fixture still fetches the distribution's checksum list and verifies the copied image before booting. A mismatched cache is refused. scripts/vm/run_integration_tests.sh is the internal VM-side runner; the controller explicitly marks that environment disposable before it may configure the private DNS/UDP test links.

docs.title: 2. QEMU/KVM Virtual Machine Orchestration
docs.text: For full kernel-level, DNS mount, and systemd integration testing, use the provided QEMU/KVM VM management scripts:

docs.title: Spawning a Test VM
docs.text:
# Launch an Arch Linux VM instance
./scripts/vm/start.sh arch

# Launch a Debian VM instance
./scripts/vm/start.sh debian

docs.title: Syncing Codebase and Taking Snapshots
docs.text:
# Sync local TTP source code into the running VM
./scripts/vm/send.sh

# Save a named VM snapshot before executing intrusive tests
./scripts/vm/snapshot.sh arch save before-fsm-test

# Restore the VM snapshot after testing completes
./scripts/vm/snapshot.sh arch restore before-fsm-test

docs.title: 3. Lifecycle Transitions in a Disposable VM
docs.text:
scripts/vm/lifecycle/run.sh takes a TTP session through shutdown, reboot and suspend/resume onto a new network, and judges each from a packet capture QEMU writes outside the guest. It needs KVM, qemu-system-x86_64, genisoimage and curl, and no root:

VM_WORK=~/.cache/ttp-lifecycle-vm scripts/vm/lifecycle/run.sh
# the same on a guest whose network is managed by NetworkManager
VM_DISTRO=fedora VM_WORK=~/.cache/ttp-lifecycle-vm-fedora scripts/vm/lifecycle/run.sh

VM_DISTRO is debian (default; Debian 13, systemd-networkd) or fedora (Fedora 44, NetworkManager, SELinux enforcing). It downloads that cloud image once (verified against the distribution's published checksum list; the list's signature is not checked), installs TTP from the working tree, and writes results.txt, one capture per phase and state snapshots into $VM_WORK. scripts/vm/lifecycle/egress.py <file.pcap> summarises a capture by destination; it streams the file, so size is not a concern. Transient download errors receive up to three retries. Downloads remain bounded by connection/transfer timeouts; checksum mismatches still fail the run. Guest readiness requires successful cloud-init completion. A timeout or error stops provisioning and records cloud-init.txt, including guest diagnostics; SSH availability alone cannot declare the VM ready. The guest preserves its image hostname. A completed cloud-init run with code 2 is accepted only if its structured report has no fatal errors and its only recoverable warnings concern setting the hostname. Other warnings, malformed evidence, installation failures and timeouts are refused; Docker must also start and answer successfully. The automated Debian downloads use the dated official build 20261103-2651 and matching dated QCOW2 filename, avoiding changes to the latest aliases. Lifecycle captures are header-only; continuous chaos observations use full frames. Both cover scenario phases, never provisioning.

scripts/vm/lifecycle/chaos.sh runs the watchdog chaos sweep (tests/chaos_monkey.py, options through CHAOS_ARGS, e.g. CHAOS_ARGS="--reset-between --no-bypass") in the same kind of guest, detached, because two of its faults cut the SSH session on purpose. It collects the log and exit code through QEMU Guest Agent over virtio-serial, independently of SSH and the guest's firewall. Failure to retrieve the result remains an error; it never counts as containment.

Both scripts run in CI from .github/workflows/lifecycle.yml. See docs/security-assessment.md section 4.3 for what it asserts and what it found.

docs.title: Required VPN with real Tor
docs.text:
scripts/vm/vpn/run.py provisions two fresh Debian 13 cloud VMs. One runs a WireGuard peer, DHCP and Internet forwarding; the other runs NetworkManager, the required VPN and TTP. Nothing changes the host's firewall or resolver. The client's provisioning NIC is disabled before measurements. QEMU Guest Agent controls the protected guest over virtio-serial, so the test needs no SSH exception in the VPN guard.

Requirements: Python 3.12+, KVM access, qemu-system-x86_64, qemu-img, genisoimage, OpenSSH and Internet access from the guests. Supply the official Debian 13 genericcloud AMD64 image and its matching published SHA512SUMS:

mkdir -p target/vpn-qualification
python3 scripts/vm/vpn/run.py \
  --base /path/to/debian-13-genericcloud-amd64.qcow2 \
  --checksums /path/to/SHA512SUMS \
  --work target/vpn-qualification/debian-unique-run

The work directory must not exist. The base image is read-only and its checksum is checked before boot; this harness does not authenticate the checksum list's signature. Obtain both from the Debian cloud image service. Source installation uses the repository's hashed dependency locks. Only tracked files are copied into the guest. Public network or Tor failures fail the run; there is no automatic fallback to an offline success.

The peer also exposes a controlled HTTP server directly on the physical path. The external QEMU capture must detect that direct path before protection and after explicit stop. During protection it accepts only ARP, DHCP and UDP to the exact VPN endpoint. Unknown traffic, fragments, truncated evidence and empty captures fail visibly. A real non-exempt HTTPS request must resolve its hostname and return IsTor=true; encrypted tunnel packets must be observed. The harness also checks DHCP renewal, tunnel loss, verified emergency containment, reconnection without reopening and explicit stop with guard removal. Each phase ends with a controlled ARP request so that even an isolated guest must produce observable link-layer traffic. This adds no IP exception. DHCP renewal requires a matching DHCPREQUEST/DHCPACK transaction, not just retries. The JSON report marks protected phases explicitly. A protected start phase counts violations from the moment the guard exists: the harness polls for inet ttp_vpn and then sends an ARP marker, and frames before it (for example the kernel's own MLD reports) are reported as before_marker. The marker trails the guard by one nft poll, a few milliseconds; a missing marker is inconclusive. Explicit stop ends the guarantee and checks guard/intent removal and zero Tor main/control PIDs; its capture may contain physical traffic from restored resolver services.

The peer also counts packets it receives, independently of any reply: cleartext requests arriving through the tunnel at an inner canary (10.9.0.1:8000, and [fd09::1]:8000 for a dual-stack tunnel), new TCP connections (SYN) it forwards to the Internet, and connections to an optional private bridge. Before protection, a request through the tunnel must increment the inner counter; while protected, application requests into the tunnel must leave it at zero. Tor's own relay traffic must increment the forwarding counter, which proves that counter can observe.

Select the underlay and tunnel families with --topology:

Topology Underlay WireGuard endpoint Tunnel and TTP flag v4-v4 (default) IPv4, DHCPv4 IPv4 IPv4, --no-ipv6 v4-dual IPv4, DHCPv4 IPv4 IPv4 and IPv6 v6-v4 IPv6, RA and stateful DHCPv6 IPv6 IPv4, --no-ipv6 v6-dual IPv6, RA and stateful DHCPv6 IPv6 IPv4 and IPv6 dual-v4 Both IPv4 IPv4, --no-ipv6 dual-dual Both IPv6 IPv4 and IPv6

For an IPv6 underlay the observer additionally accepts exactly the VPN guard's IPv6 control exceptions: DHCPv6 546 → 547 and router/neighbor solicitation or advertisement with hop limit 255. Every other IPv6 frame, including MLD, extension headers, fragments and ICMPv6 errors, is a violation while protected. Renewal requires a DHCPv6 Renew or Rebind answered by a Reply with the same transaction ID. Direct canaries are checked in every underlay family. The guests have no public IPv6 route: IPv6 is qualified on the underlay and inside the tunnel, and Tor still reaches its relays over IPv4.

After the Tor/DNS checks the harness runs ttp check six times while an unrelated nftables table is created and deleted every three seconds, which makes the watchdog re-evaluate repeatedly. Any emergency or watchdog verdict, or a latched emergency afterwards, fails the run; an inconclusive public-Tor probe (exit 3) does not. This reproduces a check that once sampled the watchdog mid-evaluation and contained a healthy session.

Right after the tunnel drops, before the watchdog latches emergency (whose table has no NAT chain), the redirect still holds and Tor cannot forward. The harness opens redirected connections there and leaves them as orphaned sockets (timed-out HTTP clients and clients closing with unread data). It targets the families TTP redirects: IPv4, and IPv6 only with a dual-stack tunnel, since --no-ipv6 drops IPv6 instead. Before explicit stop at least one orphan must still exist. After ttp stop it observes for 60 seconds: any packet to a canary or to a loopback destination on the physical link fails the run, because it belongs to a connection redirected during the session. Without the teardown's socket closure, v6-dual reproduced this leak in every run.

--bridge starts a private, unpublished obfs4 bridge on the peer and starts TTP with --use-bridges and that bridge line. Tor must verify IsTor=true while the peer counts bridge connections through the tunnel and no forwarded TCP connection: every relay connection went to the bridge. All forwarded TCP segments are reported too; a stray segment of a connection opened before the session is not a relay connection. This qualifies the managed Tor's obfs4 transport child under the VPN guard. It does not qualify snowflake, meek or the public bridge distribution.

--transitions adds suspend/resume and reboot. A continuous probe repeatedly requests the direct and tunnel canaries as root, as nobody and, on the direct route only, as Tor's UID; its unprotected control must produce visible direct packets and inner-tunnel arrivals. With protection active, the guest then suspends to RAM for longer than the DHCP lease and WireGuard's session limit, and the capture covers the whole sleep and resume. A second protected session is rebooted: QEMU pauses the guest at its reboot request, so the capture covers the entire shutdown sequence with the probe running. After boot the harness requires no retained session, guard, intent or table, then starts a new session.

The same scenarios run on relevant pull requests, weekly and on demand in .github/workflows/vpn-vm.yml, as one job per topology plus bridge and transition jobs. CI uploads reports and captures, excluding disks and seed images.

Evidence is in results.json, guest version reports, phase logs and external client/*.pcap files. Debian runs do not qualify ParrotOS, Fedora, GUI sessions, Wi-Fi roaming or real provider networks. See the VPN validation table for each gate.

docs.title: Native Parrot and AppArmor qualification
docs.text:
The same two-VM harness also accepts a separately prepared Parrot client and a native development DEB. The Debian peer remains unchanged. Optional raw UEFI code is read-only; its matching variable template is copied per guest. Disks preserve the base image's virtual size, including Parrot's 64 GiB Btrfs image.

python3 scripts/vm/vpn/run.py \
  --base /path/debian-13-genericcloud-amd64.qcow2 \
  --checksums /path/debian/SHA512SUMS \
  --client-base /path/parrot-prepared/disk.qcow2 \
  --client-checksums /path/parrot-prepared/SHA512SUMS \
  --client-os parrot --client-memory 3072 \
  --client-firmware-code /path/OVMF_CODE.fd \
  --client-firmware-vars /path/OVMF_VARS.fd \
  --client-deb packaging/transparent-tor-proxy_0.5.1_all.deb \
  --require-apparmor --work /path/new-parrot-run

The DEB filename carries the version in pyproject.toml. This command does not publish a package or tag. Build the current working tree with packaging/build_deb.sh first.

Prepare the client in a disposable overlay of the official Home image, keeping the original read-only. Verify the original signed hashes and the signing key's full fingerprint using Parrot's verification instructions. For Home 7.4, the pinned primary fingerprint is B711822346552E4D92DA02DF7A8286AF0E81EE4A. Verify the signature and fingerprint before accepting the compressed image's SHA512, then decompress it. Preserve the overlay's backing image and directory relationship; a checksum of the overlay alone does not authenticate its backing chain.

The prepared guest needs cloud-init, openssh-server, sudo and qemu-guest-agent, with SSH available for provisioning. Configure a headless multi-user.target if required by the image; preserve NetworkManager, AppArmor and distribution security settings. Install the current verified Parrot archive key if the image's packaged key has expired. Shut down the guest before hashing the prepared overlay with sha512sum disk.qcow2 > SHA512SUMS. The harness checks this derived checksum separately; retain the original signature evidence, image digest and preparation log alongside it.

With --require-apparmor, an AppArmor-free guest cannot pass. In addition to the VPN scenarios, the harness requires actual ttp-tor (enforce) evidence, starts another protected session, changes the loaded policy to complain mode inside the disposable guest, and requires the watchdog's verified emergency to identify AppArmor as its cause. Returning to enforce mode must leave the emergency latched. The external capture checks this fault phase too.

The November 2026 local qualification passed on headless Parrot Home 7.4 using the native DEB, NetworkManager 1.52.1, Tor 0.4.9.15, Python 3.13 and kernel 7.1.13+parrot7. It covered public Tor/DNS, DHCP renewal, tunnel loss/reconnection, explicit stop and the AppArmor mutation. This does not qualify GUI interaction, Secure Boot, other editions, bridge transports or other IPv6 topologies. See AppArmor's contract and limits.

Both QEMU processes are stopped on normal completion or an exception. The private work directory (mode 0700) retains disks and captures for investigation; the guest disks contain throwaway WireGuard keys. Share the reports and captures, not VM disks or cloud-init material. Captures retain the first 768 bytes of each frame, sufficient to inspect the DHCP exchange; treat them as test data.

docs.title: 4. Executing Watchdog Chaos Monkey Testing
docs.text:
The Watchdog Chaos Monkey suite simulates live system faults, abrupt process terminations, table deletions, and /etc/resolv.conf target modifications while TTP is active:

# Execute full Watchdog fault injection suite
make chaos-monkey

The VM wrapper observes all eight injections continuously on TCP, UDP and DNS in both families, including the interval before recovery audits. It retains full external captures and calibrated controls. Privileged removal of enforcement can expose traffic before repair; that exposure remains a leak in the report even when recovery succeeds. See continuous fault evidence for the exact contract, sampled cadence and artifacts. The standalone make chaos-monkey recovery audits alone do not measure this initial interval.

docs.title: Require a VPN before Tor
docs.text:
This optional feature is new in 0.5.0. The 0.5.0 release candidate passed the VM qualification gates listed in the validation limits below.

The supported order is user → VPN → Tor → destination. TTP's Tor connects to its guards or bridges through the VPN; websites still see a Tor exit. Combining VPN and Tor does not automatically improve anonymity. The VPN knows your source address and can observe connections to Tor. This does not prevent traffic correlation, browser fingerprinting, account identification, or a privileged administrator changing the host. See the Tor Project advice and Whonix's comparison.

docs.title: Supported configuration and prerequisites
docs.text:
Requirement Initial contract VPN backend Native NetworkManager WireGuard; already active before TTP Selection Explicit NetworkManager connection UUID; no guessing by interface name Peers Exactly one, with a numeric fixed IP and port Routing Full IPv4 tunnel; full IPv6 tunnel or explicit --no-ipv6 Physical underlay Ordinary Ethernet/Wi-Fi, VM Ethernet or veth; VLAN, bridge, bond and other virtual underlays are refused in the initial implementation Supervision Watchdog required; optional desktop notifications remain independent Service teardown Unified cgroup v2; retain protection until the managed Tor cgroup is empty Tor Dedicated TTP-managed instance, including its bridge transport children Bypasses No root, UID/GID, cgroup or LAN bypass Ownership VPN configuration, credentials, activation and shutdown remain with the user/VPN manager

OpenVPN, provider applications, wg-quick, VPN-after-Tor, split-tunnel VPNs, multiple VPNs/peers, endpoint hostnames/roaming, and external Tor daemons are outside the initial contract. A VPN client which flushes unrelated firewall tables is incompatible. Containers, forwarded clients and gateway deployments are not covered by this mode; forwarding is blocked.

Applications with network administration or raw-packet capabilities require separate trust. In particular, the mark/endpoint exception identifies allowed WireGuard transport packets, not an authenticated application identity. Do not use this mode as a sandbox for privileged pentesting tools or malicious root processes; they can manipulate networking or exploit control-traffic exceptions.

Install NetworkManager, WireGuard tools (wg), iproute2 (ip) and systemd's busctl using the distribution package manager if absent. These are optional mode dependencies; TTP does not install them. Existing TTP dependencies still apply. NetworkManager's selected peer must have full-tunnel AllowedIPs, a live nonzero WireGuard fwmark, and consistent kernel settings. TTP refuses ambiguous or changed evidence instead of rewriting the profile or routing policy.

docs.title: Start the session
docs.text:
Configure and activate the VPN using your existing trusted workflow. TTP does not import a provider configuration or fetch credentials. Inspect public profile identities with:

nmcli -f NAME,UUID,TYPE,DEVICE connection show --active

Then select that connection explicitly (replace the sample UUID):

sudo ttp start --require-vpn 12345678-1234-4234-8234-123456789012 \
  --watchdog --no-lan-bypass --no-ipv6

Omit --no-ipv6 only when the selected VPN covers IPv6 as well. Add --notifications if you want optional desktop delivery. For direct root invocations, select a notification recipient as described in Supervision and notifications.

Missing or unsupported VPN evidence returns 10 before network changes. The effective path, device indices, active-connection identity, public peer, endpoint and mark are frozen for the session. TTP never requests NetworkManager GetSecrets or reads WireGuard private/preshared keys. Do not use wg ... dump in diagnostic reports: it can include secrets.

docs.title: What enforces the path
docs.text:
Before starting Tor, TTP records private recovery intent and installs a separate inet ttp_vpn table. It permits loopback, the Tor UID on the frozen tunnel device, and narrowly scoped WireGuard outer packets to the frozen endpoint on the frozen physical device. Other application egress and forwarding are blocked even before the main transparent-proxy rules exist. The normal TTP table gets the same transport exceptions and disables cgroup bypass rules.

The underlay exceptions also allow root-owned DHCPv4 client traffic (68 → 67), DHCPv6 client traffic (546 → 547), and IPv6 router solicitation/neighbor discovery with hop limit 255 on the frozen underlay. They are network control traffic, not a general root exemption. ARP is outside the inet ruleset. Do not interpret this mode as a promise that no unencapsulated physical packet exists.

The independent table uses explicit postrouting/forward hooks, priorities and drop policies. Its verification compares kernel JSON against the expected frozen specification. An observed ruleset hash is not adopted as the specification. Interface names in the kernel response are resolved back to their indices, so recreating an interface with the same name does not inherit trust. The egress check runs after routing: in OUTPUT a redirected TCP connection can still expose its original tunnel interface even though its destination has become Tor's loopback listener. Checking the final device avoids blocking that connection without allowing application packets onto the tunnel or underlay.

The protection does not depend on a polling check noticing a route change: Tor packets routed to the physical link are already forbidden. The required watchdog adds bounded observation and emergency response; process scheduling prevents a promise of immediate notification or instantaneous fault detection.

docs.title: Observe evidence and respond to a fault
docs.text:
sudo ttp status
sudo ttp status --json
sudo ttp monitor

VPN state constrained means the current local profile/device/routing evidence agrees with the frozen policy and the independent kernel rules were verified. It does not prove a recent successful provider handshake or continuous remote reachability. A tunnel may retain its interface and routes while the remote peer is unreachable. The VPN state and guard_verified are independent: a disconnected profile can be unknown while the kernel guard is still present.

The JSON field handshake_at is the last recorded WireGuard handshake in Unix wall-clock seconds (null when none), not a new connectivity measurement. The existing rejected-packet counter belongs to the main TTP table; it does not count packets dropped by the independent VPN guard.

ttp check deliberately performs a new Tor verification. A result IsTor=true does not by itself prove a VPN path. If the required VPN evidence is unavailable, the check requests emergency containment before attempting an external probe. status and monitor remain passive. Desktop notifications contain concise incidents without the public peer key, endpoint or credentials.

Disconnect, profile reactivation, changed device index, changed endpoint/mark, an observed route fallback or missing/altered guard causes the watchdog to request emergency containment. A NetworkManager restart or underlay interface replacement may therefore require a fresh TTP session. No other VPN or direct Tor connection is silently substituted. Failure to read evidence is unknown.

Emergency containment blocks input, output and forwarding except loopback, including VPN reconnection traffic. A reconnected VPN does not reopen the session. Existing emergency requested/applied/verified evidence and exit codes 7/8 still apply; the VPN diagnostic is retained alongside other causes.

docs.title: Stop and recover deliberately
docs.text:
Close sensitive applications first. After stopping TTP those applications can communicate without Tor, and may use the physical network if the external VPN is down or later disconnects.

sudo ttp stop

TTP stops its watchdog and managed Tor, restores its normal firewall/DNS changes, verifies Tor has no systemd main/control process or populated cgroup, and removes the VPN guard last. It leaves the externally managed VPN alone. ttp restart refuses required-VPN sessions before teardown because stop/start has an unprotected interval. Use explicit stop and then start only after closing sensitive work.

An interrupted startup can leave vpn-intent.json and kernel protection even without a normal session lock. status reports retained protection and a new start refuses to adopt it. Use:

sudo ttp stop --restore-only

If Tor termination or kernel inspection is unconfirmed, protection is retained and recovery fails visibly. Inspect journalctl -u ttp-tor -u ttp-watchdog and sudo nft list table inet ttp_vpn. Do not delete the guard merely to clear a startup error while Tor might still be running. Preserve console access for recovery: this mode can intentionally disconnect the host.

The session does not survive reboot. TTP's Tor unit, runtime intent and tables are volatile; after reboot TTP makes no Tor or VPN guarantee. Your VPN's own autostart policy is separate. During the shutdown itself the guard remains in the kernel: qualification observed no direct packet until the guest powered off, with a probe trying direct and tunnel paths throughout. A new session starts after boot without --restore-only.

Suspend ends the session in emergency. On sleep, NetworkManager deactivates the physical connection and reactivates it on wake. The frozen path is then briefly unavailable, so the watchdog latches verified emergency containment even though the WireGuard device itself survives. Nothing leaves directly during sleep or resume, and the host stays offline until you run sudo ttp stop and start a new session. This is intentional fail-closed behavior, not a fault to work around; close sensitive applications before stopping.

docs.text:
Qualification Status Adversarial profile, CLI and recovery unit tests Implemented Real NM/WireGuard, independent capture and guard-removal mutation Implemented in offline container fixture IPv6 payload/outer transport, required watchdog and explicit stop Implemented with TTP_VPN_DUALSTACK=1 Public Tor startup and DNS, IPv4 underlay/tunnel Implemented in the external QEMU VM fixture DHCPv4 renewal with matching request/ACK and retained emergency across reconnect Implemented in the external QEMU VM fixture IPv4, IPv6 and dual-stack underlays (DHCPv4, RA and stateful DHCPv6 renewal) with IPv4 or IPv6 endpoints, IPv4 or dual-stack tunnels Qualified in Debian 13 VMs: six topologies, no cleartext application traffic into the tunnel Private obfs4 bridge through the tunnel, transport child confined by ttp-tor Qualified in Debian 13 VMs; snowflake, meek and public bridges not qualified Suspend/resume and reboot with a continuous probe Qualified in Debian 13 VMs: resume latches emergency; shutdown keeps the guard until power-off ParrotOS Home 7.4: native DEB, NetworkManager, AppArmor enforce, IPv4 underlay/tunnel Qualified locally (November 2026); other topologies, bridges and transitions run on Debian only Real providers, Wi-Fi roaming, GUI sessions, Fedora Not qualified

scripts/check-vpn.sh runs a real NetworkManager/WireGuard tunnel and local peer inside a disposable offline systemd container. Capture is on the peer's physical side. Positive controls and deliberate removal of the VPN guard prove the observer can detect the prohibited direct path. It also tests route fallback, reconnection with changed identity, coexistence with the TTP table and retained protection while a systemd Tor test process is live.

That fixture uses a controlled Tor UID probe, not a public Tor circuit. The VM qualification below adds actual TTP startup and Tor verification through the tunnel, DNS interception, the IPv4/IPv6 combinations, bridges, transport failures, emergency latching, stop/recovery and suspend/reboot, with an observer outside the guest.

The QEMU qualification recipe runs real Tor with non-exempt hostname-based HTTPS verification, DHCP/DHCPv6 renewal, tunnel loss and emergency persistence after reconnection. It captures the client's physical path outside the guest and counts, at the peer, any cleartext application request that enters the tunnel. Cleartext controls must be reachable before protection and after explicit stop. The stop phase ends protection intentionally; restored resolver/network services may then emit ordinary physical traffic.

Limits of that evidence: the guests have no public IPv6 route, so IPv6 is measured on the underlay and inside the tunnel while Tor reaches relays over IPv4; a successful Tor request over IPv6 is not demonstrated. The bridge is a private obfs4 bridge on the test peer. Suspend uses QEMU S3 with NetworkManager's default sleep handling. Each scenario observes only the intervals it ran.

The architecture follows Whonix's VPN-before-Tor fail-closed principle and the Qubes community VPN gateway design. Their gateway rules are not copied onto a TTP host. Technical references: WireGuard routing, NetworkManager non-secret settings API, and nftables hook/verdict behavior.

def apply_rules(
    tor_user: str,
    transport_port: int = 9041,
    dns_port: int = 9054,
    allow_root: bool = False,
    lan_bypass: bool = True,
    bypass_uids: list[int] | None = None,
    bypass_gids: list[int] | None = None,
    disable_ipv6: bool = False,
    vpn: dict | None = None,
) -> None:
    """Create the dedicated 'inet ttp' table and inject redirection rules.

    Create Table -> Flush Table -> Apply Ruleset is submitted to nft as a single
    transaction, so the table is never observable in a half-applied state.
    If any step fails, triggers an automatic rollback (table destruction).

    Args:
        tor_user: Username or numeric UID string of the Tor daemon process.
        transport_port: Local TCP port for Tor TransPort redirection.
        dns_port: Local UDP/TCP port for Tor DNSPort redirection.
        allow_root: If True, allows processes running as root (UID 0) to bypass rules.
        lan_bypass: If True, excludes local LAN subnets from redirection.
        bypass_uids: Optional list of numeric UIDs exempted from redirection.
        bypass_gids: Optional list of numeric GIDs exempted from redirection.
        disable_ipv6: If True, forces dropping all IPv6 traffic regardless of host availability.

    Raises:
        FirewallError: If the tor_user is invalid or rule injection fails.
    """
    # Resolve numeric UID for the tor user to avoid nft resolution issues
    try:
        tor_uid = int(tor_user) if tor_user.isdigit() else pwd.getpwnam(tor_user).pw_uid
    except KeyError as e:
        raise FirewallError(f"Tor user '{tor_user}' not found on system.") from e

    from ttp.tor_detect import is_ipv6_supported

    ipv6_avail = is_ipv6_supported() and not disable_ipv6

    # Resolve systemd-resolved UID once, before building the ruleset
    resolved_uid: int | None = None
    for _user in ("systemd-resolve", "systemd-resolved"):
        try:
            resolved_uid = pwd.getpwnam(_user).pw_uid
            break
        except KeyError:
            continue

    vpn_rules = ""
    if vpn is not None:
        from ttp.vpn import VPNPolicy
        from ttp.vpn_guard import transport_rules

        vpn_rules = transport_rules(VPNPolicy.from_snapshot(vpn))

    ruleset = _build_ruleset(
        tor_uid=tor_uid,
        transport_port=transport_port,
        dns_port=dns_port,
        ipv6_avail=ipv6_avail,
        allow_root=allow_root,
        lan_bypass=lan_bypass,
        bypass_uids=bypass_uids,
        bypass_gids=bypass_gids,
        resolved_uid=resolved_uid,
        cgroup_bypass=False if vpn is not None else _has_cgroup_bypass_support(),
        vpn_transport=vpn_rules,
    )

    try:
        _apply_table_atomically(ruleset)
        logger.info(f"Stateless rules applied. Tor user ({tor_user}, UID {tor_uid}) is exempt.")
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Firewall injection failed: {e}. Rolling back...")
        destroy_rules()
        if not isinstance(e, FirewallError):
            raise FirewallError(f"Failed to apply stateless rules: {e}") from e
        raise

Destroy the 'ttp' table and clean up firewall rules.

This is the atomic cleanup operation. It flushes the table, destroys it, and verifies that the table is no longer present in kernel state.

Returns:

Name Type Description bool bool

True if the table was successfully destroyed or already gone.

Raises:

Type Description FirewallError

If table destruction fails and the table remains active.

def destroy_rules() -> bool:
    """Destroy the 'ttp' table and clean up firewall rules.

    This is the atomic cleanup operation. It flushes the table, destroys it,
    and verifies that the table is no longer present in kernel state.

    Returns:
        bool: True if the table was successfully destroyed or already gone.

    Raises:
        FirewallError: If table destruction fails and the table remains active.
    """
    # Flush the table first for absolute cleanup safety
    subprocess.run(
        [resolve("nft"), "flush", "table", "inet", "ttp"],
        capture_output=True,
        check=False,
        timeout=10,
    )
    # `delete` is supported by older nft versions (including 1.0.6), unlike
    # `destroy`. The existence check below supplies idempotence when absent.
    result = subprocess.run(
        [resolve("nft"), "delete", "table", "inet", "ttp"],
        capture_output=True,
        check=False,
        timeout=10,
    )
    # returncode 1 with table absent = already clean, not an error
    # to distinguish it, check if the table exists
    # Remove any ruleset file left behind by an older version, on every exit
    # path: TTP no longer writes one (the ruleset is piped to `nft -f -`), and
    # a stale copy of a session's ports, UIDs and bypass list should not
    # outlive the session.
    RULES_TEMP_PATH.unlink(missing_ok=True)

    if result.returncode != 0:
        # Check: does the table still exist?
        check = subprocess.run(
            [resolve("nft"), "list", "table", "inet", "ttp"],
            capture_output=True,
            check=False,
            timeout=10,
        )
        if check.returncode != 0:
            # The table is gone - destroy "failed" because it was already clean
            return True
        # The table still exists - destroy actually failed
        err_msg = result.stderr.decode().strip() if result.stderr else "unknown error"
        logger.error(f"nft delete failed: {err_msg}")
        raise FirewallError(f"Failed to destroy nftables ruleset: {err_msg}")

    return True

docs.title: read_counters()
docs.text:
Return the packet count of each named counter in inet ttp.

Empty when the table is absent or nft cannot be reached, so a caller that cannot measure is never handed a zero it might read as evidence.

Source code in ttp/firewall/runner.py 
def read_counters() -> dict[str, int]:
    """Return the packet count of each named counter in ``inet ttp``.

    Empty when the table is absent or nft cannot be reached, so a caller that
    cannot measure is never handed a zero it might read as evidence.
    """
    try:
        res = subprocess.run(
            [resolve("nft"), "-j", "list", "counters", "table", "inet", "ttp"],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            check=True,
            timeout=10,
        )
    except (OSError, subprocess.CalledProcessError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired):
        return {}

    try:
        payload = json.loads(res.stdout)
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, ValueError):
        return {}

    counters: dict[str, int] = {}
    for entry in payload.get("nftables", []):
        counter = entry.get("counter") if isinstance(entry, dict) else None
        if isinstance(counter, dict) and "name" in counter:
            try:
                counters[str(counter["name"])] = int(counter.get("packets", 0))
            except (TypeError, ValueError):
                continue
    return counters

-s (stateless) leaves counter values out, so the fingerprint changes when the rules do and not when traffic moves a counter. ttp start records it in the lock and the watchdog compares against it (#80): a table can keep every chain name - a flush does - while holding no rules at all.

def table_fingerprint() -> str | None:
    """SHA-256 of `nft -s list table inet ttp`, or ``None`` if the table cannot be read.

    ``-s`` (stateless) leaves counter values out, so the fingerprint changes when
    the rules do and not when traffic moves a counter. ``ttp start`` records it
    in the lock and the watchdog compares against it (#80): a table can keep
    every chain name - a flush does - while holding no rules at all.
    """
    try:
        res = subprocess.run(
            [resolve("nft"), "-s", "list", "table", "inet", "ttp"],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            check=False,
            timeout=10,
        )
    except (OSError, subprocess.TimeoutExpired):
        return None
    if res.returncode != 0:
        return None
    return hashlib.sha256(res.stdout.encode()).hexdigest()

                "inet",
                "ttp",
                "filter_out",
                "meta",
                "l4proto",
                "udp",
                "counter",
                "reject",

        # 2. Kill pending TCP connections instantly (sends RST to the local process)
        _run_nft(

                "insert",

                "filter_out",
                "meta",
                "l4proto",
                "tcp",
                "counter",
                "reject",
                "with",

def apply_emergency_killswitch(*, timeout: float = 10) -> None:
    """Apply an emergency network killswitch.

    Replaces the 'inet ttp' table with an ultra-restrictive ruleset that drops
    all inbound, outbound, and forwarded network traffic on physical interfaces,
    permitting only local loopback communication.

    Raises:
        FirewallError: If table creation or killswitch ruleset injection fails.
    """
    ruleset = """
    table inet ttp {
        chain filter_out {
            type filter hook output priority filter; policy drop;
            oifname "lo" accept
        }
        chain filter_forward {
            type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop;
        }
        chain filter_input {
            type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop;
            iifname "lo" accept
        }
    }
    """
    try:
        # Table reset and drop-all ruleset go in as one transaction. Flushing in a
        # separate nft call would briefly leave the table empty, which is an open
        # network at the exact moment integrity has already been lost.
        _apply_table_atomically(ruleset, timeout=timeout)
        logger.warning("Emergency rules application accepted; kernel verification is still required.")
    except Exception as e:
        logger.error(f"Failed to apply emergency killswitch: {e}")
        if not isinstance(e, FirewallError):
            raise FirewallError(f"Failed to apply emergency killswitch: {e}") from e
        raise

def apply_teardown_lockdown(tor_uid: int | None = None) -> None:
    """Insert a lockdown drop rule at the top of the filter_out chain in table inet ttp.

    Ensures all non-loopback outbound traffic is dropped during graceful session teardown,
    while permitting the Tor daemon UID to close control connections cleanly.

    Args:
        tor_uid: Optional numeric UID of the Tor daemon process to exempt from lockdown.
    """
    rule = ["insert", "rule", "inet", "ttp", "filter_out"]
    if tor_uid is not None:
        # nft joins its non-option argv into a single buffer and lexes it
        # line-wise, so a newline or ';' inside one argument starts another
        # nft command. This value comes from the session lock, so it must be
        # proved to be a plain non-negative integer before it is formatted in.
        try:
            uid = int(tor_uid)
        except (TypeError, ValueError):
            raise ValueError(f"tor_uid must be an integer, got {tor_uid!r}")
        if uid < 0:
            raise ValueError(f"tor_uid must be non-negative, got {uid}")
        rule += ["meta", "skuid", "!=", str(uid)]
    rule += ["oifname", "!=", "lo", "drop"]

    try:
        _run_nft(rule)
        logger.warning("Teardown lockdown applied: outbound traffic locked.")
    except Exception as e:
        _log_teardown_failure("Teardown lockdown", e)

def generate_torrc(
    tor_user: str,
    transport_port: int = 9041,
    dns_port: int = 9054,
    block_doh: bool = True,
    use_bridges: bool = False,
    bridges: Optional[list[str]] = None,
    disable_ipv6: bool = False,
) -> Path:
    """Generate a volatile ``torrc`` in ``/run/tor/ttp/torrc``.

    The ``DataDirectory`` points to the persistent cache (``/var/lib/tor/ttp``)
    so that Entry Guards are preserved across runs for fast bootstrapping.

    Args:
        tor_user: Username running the Tor process.
        transport_port: Local TCP port for Tor TransPort redirection.
        dns_port: Local UDP/TCP port for Tor DNSPort redirection.
        block_doh: If True, maps well-known DoH resolver domains to 0.0.0.0.
        use_bridges: If True, configures Tor to route via Pluggable Transports.
        bridges: Optional list of bridge lines (e.g. ``["obfs4 ...", "snowflake ..."]``).
        disable_ipv6: If True, forces IPv6 client routing off.

    Returns:
        Path: Absolute path to the generated ``torrc`` file.
    """
    # mkdir's mode is filtered by the invoking root's umask.  A new /run/tor
    # must remain searchable by the service account; the child carrying the
    # configuration and cookie remains private.  Leave existing distro-owned
    # parents alone.
    if not TOR_RUNTIME_DIR.parent.exists():
        TOR_RUNTIME_DIR.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        os.chmod(TOR_RUNTIME_DIR.parent, 0o755)
    TOR_RUNTIME_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    try:
        shutil.chown(TOR_RUNTIME_DIR, user=tor_user, group=tor_user)
    except (KeyError, ValueError, OSError):
        pass
    os.chmod(TOR_RUNTIME_DIR, 0o700)

    # Ensure parent directory of cache is owned by the Tor user and has correct permissions
    parent_dir = TOR_CACHE_DIR.parent
    if parent_dir.exists():
        try:
            shutil.chown(parent_dir, user=tor_user, group=tor_user)
            os.chmod(parent_dir, 0o700)
        except (KeyError, ValueError, OSError):
            pass

    # Persistent cache directory must be fixed on every run
    data_dir = str(TOR_CACHE_DIR)
    os.makedirs(data_dir, exist_ok=True)
    try:
        shutil.chown(data_dir, user=tor_user)
    except (KeyError, ValueError, OSError):
        pass
    os.chmod(data_dir, 0o700)

    from ttp.tor_detect import is_ipv6_supported

    ipv6_avail = is_ipv6_supported() and not disable_ipv6

    torrc_content = _build_torrc_content(
        tor_user=tor_user,
        transport_port=transport_port,
        dns_port=dns_port,
        block_doh=block_doh,
        use_bridges=use_bridges,
        bridges=bridges,
        ipv6_avail=ipv6_avail,
    )

    torrc_path = TOR_RUNTIME_DIR / "torrc"
    _write_private(torrc_path, torrc_content)
    logger.info("Generated runtime torrc at %s", torrc_path)
    return torrc_path

def start_tor_service(
    tor_user: str,
    transport_port: int = 9041,
    dns_port: int = 9054,
    block_doh: bool = True,
    use_bridges: bool = False,
    bridges: Optional[list[str]] = None,
    disable_ipv6: bool = False,
) -> dict | None:
    """Generate the runtime torrc and start a dedicated TTP Tor systemd service.

    Sequence:
        1. Generate volatile torrc in ``/run/tor/ttp/torrc``.
        2. Label SELinux ports if SELinux is enforcing.
        3. Write a volatile ``ttp-tor.service`` unit to ``/run/systemd/system/``.
        4. Reload systemd daemon and start the service.

    Args:
        tor_user: System user designated to run Tor.
        transport_port: Local TCP port for Tor TransPort redirection.
        dns_port: Local UDP/TCP port for Tor DNSPort redirection.
        block_doh: If True, maps canary DoH domains to 0.0.0.0.
        use_bridges: If True, configures Tor to route via Pluggable Transports.
        bridges: Optional list of bridge configuration strings.
        disable_ipv6: If True, forces IPv6 client routing off.

    Raises:
        TorError: If systemd daemon reload or service restart fails.
    """
    generate_torrc(
        tor_user,
        transport_port=transport_port,
        dns_port=dns_port,
        block_doh=block_doh,
        use_bridges=use_bridges,
        bridges=bridges,
        disable_ipv6=disable_ipv6,
    )
    label_ports_selinux(transport_port, dns_port)
    confinement = apparmor.prepare()
    if confinement is None:
        _write_service_unit(tor_user)
    else:
        _write_service_unit(tor_user, apparmor.PROFILE)

    try:
        subprocess.run(
            [resolve("systemctl"), "daemon-reload"],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            check=True,
        )
        subprocess.run(
            [resolve("systemctl"), "restart", TTP_SERVICE_NAME],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            check=True,
        )
    except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
        detail = (e.stderr or "").strip()
        message = f"Failed to start '{TTP_SERVICE_NAME}': {detail}"
        # systemctl says only that the job failed. The reason Tor refused to
        # run is in its own journal, and it is the whole point of failing here
        # rather than 60s later: "Could not bind to 127.0.0.1:9054: Permission
        # denied" tells an operator what to do, "Job for ttp-tor.service
        # failed" does not.
        journal = _recent_journal()
        if journal:
            message += f"\nLast lines from the Tor journal:\n{journal}"
        raise TorError(message) from e
    if confinement is not None:
        observation = apparmor.observe(confinement, pwd.getpwnam(tor_user).pw_uid)
        if observation["state"] != "enforced":
            stop_tor_service()
            raise TorError(f"Required Tor AppArmor confinement could not be verified. See {apparmor.GUIDE}")
    logger.info("TTP Tor service started with dedicated config.")
    return confinement

    If any required binary is missing, displays distro package guidance and official
    Tor documentation links, then exits with status code 1. Nothing is installed.

            from ttp.commands._common import _PREFIX, console

            console.print(f"{_PREFIX} [bold red]Unsupported pluggable transport: '{pt}'[/bold red]")

        pt_info = PT_MAP[pt]

                pkg_debian=pt_info["apt-get"],
                pkg_fedora=pt_info["dnf"],
                pkg_arch=pt_info["pacman"],

    transport_port: int = 9041,
    dns_port: int = 9054,
    block_doh: bool = True,
    use_bridges: bool = False,
    bridges: Optional[list[str]] = None,
    disable_ipv6: bool = False,
    before_start: Callable[[str], None] | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Ensure Tor is installed and start it via the dedicated systemd service.

    Enforces a strict NO AUTO-INSTALL policy. If Tor or required helper binaries are missing,
    displays distro-aware installation guidance and exits with status code 1.

    Args:
        transport_port: Local TCP port for Tor TransPort redirection.
        dns_port: Local UDP/TCP port for Tor DNSPort redirection.
        block_doh: If True, blocks known DoH resolvers in firewall and torrc.
        use_bridges: If True, enables Pluggable Transport bridges.
        bridges: Optional list of bridge configuration strings.
        disable_ipv6: If True, forces IPv6 client routing off.

    Returns:
        dict[str, Any]: Dictionary containing detected Tor installation metadata.

    Raises:
        typer.Exit: With exit code 1 if Tor binary is not installed on the system.
    """
    info = detect_tor(transport_port=transport_port, dns_port=dns_port)

    if not info["is_installed"]:
        cmd = _get_distro_install_command(pkg_debian="tor", pkg_fedora="tor")
        doc_url = "https://community.torproject.org/onion-services/setup/install/"

        msg = (

            "[bold cyan]Recommended installation command:[/bold cyan]\n"
            f"  [bold yellow]{cmd}[/bold yellow]\n\n"
            "[bold cyan]Official Tor Project Installation Guide:[/bold cyan]\n"
            f"  {doc_url}"
        )
        from ttp.commands._common import console

        console.print(Panel(msg, title="[bold red]Missing Tor Dependency[/bold red]", expand=False))
        raise typer.Exit(code=1)

    tor_user = info.get("tor_user", "debian-tor")
    _assert_is_tor_system_account(tor_user)

    # If bridges are requested, ensure the corresponding pluggable transports are installed
    if use_bridges and bridges:
        required_transports = []
        for b in bridges:
            parts = b.split()
            if parts:
                first_word = parts[0].lower()
                if first_word in PT_MAP and first_word not in required_transports:
                    required_transports.append(first_word)
        if required_transports:
            ensure_pluggable_transports(required_transports)

    if before_start is not None:
        before_start(tor_user)

    # Start Tor via the dedicated ttp-tor service
    confinement = start_tor_service(
        tor_user,
        transport_port=transport_port,
        dns_port=dns_port,
        block_doh=block_doh,
        use_bridges=use_bridges,
        bridges=bridges,
        disable_ipv6=disable_ipv6,
    )

    if isinstance(confinement, dict):
        info["apparmor"] = confinement
    return info

def get_controller():
    """Connect to the dedicated ``ttp-tor`` control interface only.

    Uses exclusively ``ControlSocket /run/tor/ttp/control.sock`` so
    bootstrap queries, NEWNYM, and shutdown signals always target TTP's
    isolated instance - never ``tor.service`` or TCP ControlPort.
    Returns an authenticated :class:`stem.control.Controller` or ``None``.
    """
    if Controller is None:
        return None

    if not os.path.exists(_TTP_CONTROL_SOCKET):
        return None

    import stem
    import stem.connection

    try:
        ctrl = Controller.from_socket_file(_TTP_CONTROL_SOCKET)
        ctrl.authenticate()
        return ctrl
    except (OSError, stem.SocketError) as e:
        logger.debug("Tor control socket not reachable: %s", e)
        return None
    except stem.connection.AuthenticationFailure as e:
        logger.error("Tor control socket authentication failed: %s", e)
        return None
    except stem.ControllerError as e:
        logger.warning("Tor controller error: %s", e)
        return None

def get_exit_ip() -> str:
    """Fetch the current Tor exit IP, trying multiple endpoints for resilience.

    Uses ``urllib.request`` from the stdlib so we don't need to add
    ``requests`` as a dependency.
    """
    saw_reply = False
    for endpoint in VERIFY_ENDPOINTS:
        data = _fetch_endpoint(endpoint)
        if data is not None:
            saw_reply = True
            # check.torproject.org uses "IP", ipify uses "ip", ifconfig.me uses "ip_addr"
            ip = _canonical_ip(data.get("IP") or data.get("ip") or data.get("ip_addr"))
            if ip is not None:
                return ip
            logger.warning("Endpoint %s returned a value that is not an IP address; ignoring.", endpoint)
    # A reply that is not an address is not the same as no reply: callers
    # branch on NO_ANSWER to report "could not reach any endpoint".
    return MALFORMED_ANSWER if saw_reply else NO_ANSWER

def graceful_shutdown(timeout: int = 10) -> bool:
    """Send ``SHUTDOWN`` signal to Tor for clean circuit teardown.

    This MUST be called **before** firewall teardown to avoid leaking
    cleartext RST packets on the physical interface.  Tor will close
    all circuits cryptographically, then exit.

    Parameters
    ----------
    timeout:
        Maximum seconds to wait for Tor to finish closing circuits.

    Returns
    -------
    bool
        ``True`` if the shutdown signal was sent successfully.
    """
    if Signal is None:
        return False

    ctrl = get_controller()
    if ctrl is None:
        return False

    import stem

    try:
        with ctrl:
            ctrl.signal(Signal.SHUTDOWN)

        # Wait for Tor to finish closing circuits
        for _ in range(timeout):
            ctrl_check = get_controller()
            if ctrl_check is None:
                return True
            try:
                ctrl_check.close()
            except (OSError, stem.ControllerError):
                pass
            time.sleep(1)
        return True
    except (OSError, stem.ControllerError):
        return False

def request_new_circuit() -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """Request a new Tor circuit (new exit IP) and wait for it to change.

    Returns
    -------
    tuple[bool, str]
        ``(ip_changed, current_ip)``
    """
    old_ip = get_exit_ip()

    ctrl = get_controller()
    if ctrl is None:
        raise TorError("Cannot connect to Tor control interface. Check that Tor is running.")

    import stem

    try:
        with ctrl:
            ctrl.signal(Signal.NEWNYM)
    except (OSError, stem.ControllerError) as e:
        raise TorError(f"Failed to request new circuit from Tor controller: {e}") from e

    new_ip = old_ip

    # Poll for IP change instead of fixed sleep
    for _ in range(12):  # max ~60s
        time.sleep(5)
        new_ip = get_exit_ip()
        if new_ip != old_ip and new_ip != "unknown":
            return True, new_ip

    return False, new_ip

def verify_tor() -> tuple[bool, str]:
    """Verify that traffic is actually routed through Tor.

    Tries multiple endpoints for resilience. The Tor Project's API is
    authoritative (it returns ``IsTor``); the fallback endpoints only
    confirm we can reach the internet through *some* exit node.

    Returns
    -------
    tuple[bool, str]
        ``(is_tor, exit_ip)`` - whether we confirmed Tor routing,
        and the exit IP address.
    """
    # What a fallback reported, kept rather than returned: a fallback cannot
    # decide the verdict, so answering first must not end the attempts either.
    # Returning it at once meant one slow answer from check.torproject.org -
    # routine for Tor clients, and likeliest on a freshly built circuit - was
    # final, and the remaining attempts never asked the authority again.
    fallback_ip: str | None = None
    for _attempt in range(1, 6):  # 5 attempts
        for endpoint in VERIFY_ENDPOINTS:
            data = _fetch_endpoint(endpoint)
            if data is None:
                continue

            # Only the Tor Project API is authoritative for IsTor, and only
            # because of which URL answered -- not because a field of that
            # name is present. The fallbacks are ordinary IP echo services:
            # whatever keys they put in their body, they may report an
            # address, never assert Tor routing.
            if endpoint == VERIFY_ENDPOINTS[0]:
                if "IsTor" in data:
                    return bool(data.get("IsTor", False)), _canonical_ip(data.get("IP")) or MALFORMED_ANSWER
                # Trusted origin, unexpected shape: do not upgrade the verdict,
                # and do not let a fallback speak for it either.
                return False, _canonical_ip(data.get("IP")) or MALFORMED_ANSWER

            # Fallback endpoints: we got a response, so traffic is routed
            # through *something*. We can't confirm it's Tor, but we have an IP.
            ip = _canonical_ip(data.get("ip") or data.get("ip_addr"))
            fallback_ip = ip if ip is not None else fallback_ip or MALFORMED_ANSWER
            break  # one reflector per attempt is enough; ask the authority again next time
        time.sleep(3)

    if fallback_ip is not None:
        logger.warning("check.torproject.org did not answer in 5 attempts; exit IP from a fallback only.")
        return False, fallback_ip
    return False, NO_ANSWER

def wait_for_bootstrap(progress_callback: Optional[Callable[[int], None]] = None, timeout: int = 180) -> bool:
    """Wait for Tor to reach 100% bootstrap status via ControlPort.

    Parameters
    ----------
    progress_callback:
        Optional callable that takes an integer (0-100) representing
        the bootstrap percentage.
    """
    # 1. Wait for the control interface to be available (up to 60s).
    controller = None
    bootstrap_conn_timeout = 60
    for _ in range(bootstrap_conn_timeout // 2):
        controller = get_controller()
        if controller is not None:
            break
        time.sleep(2)

    if not controller:
        raise TorError(f"Could not connect to Tor control interface after {bootstrap_conn_timeout}s.")

    # 2. Monitor bootstrap progress.
    import stem

    try:
        with controller:
            for _ in range(timeout):  # Use the provided timeout (default 90)
                status = controller.get_info("status/bootstrap-phase")
                match = re.search(r"PROGRESS=(\d+)", status)
                progress_val = int(match.group(1)) if match else 0

                if progress_callback:
                    progress_callback(progress_val)

                if "PROGRESS=100" in status:
                    return True

                time.sleep(1)

            raise TorError("Tor bootstrap timed out.")
    except (OSError, stem.ControllerError) as e:
        raise TorError(f"Tor control socket communication failed during bootstrap: {e}") from e

def apply_dns(interface: str, disable_ipv6: bool = False, dns_port: int = 9054) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Apply Tor DNS settings using a Kernel-level overlay (mount --bind).

    If systemd-resolved is active, also writes a volatile drop-in configuration
    and restarts it via the ttp.dns_resolved module.

    Returns a dictionary containing backup data for restoration.
    """
    resolved_active = False
    try:
        from ttp import dns_resolved
        from ttp.system_info import is_ipv6_supported

        # Configure systemd-resolved if active
        resolved_active = dns_resolved.apply_resolved(dns_port=dns_port, disable_ipv6=disable_ipv6)

        nameservers = "nameserver 127.0.0.1\n"
        if is_ipv6_supported() and not disable_ipv6:
            nameservers += "nameserver ::1\n"

        # 1. Write the Tor resolver to /run/ttp/resolv.conf (volatile).
        #    O_NOFOLLOW refuses a symlink planted at this name outright: without
        #    it, root truncates and overwrites whatever the link points at, and
        #    restore_dns() unlinks this file at teardown, so the name is free
        #    between sessions and no race is needed to plant one.
        RUNTIME_RESOLV.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        fd = os.open(
            str(RUNTIME_RESOLV),
            os.O_WRONLY | os.O_CREAT | os.O_TRUNC | os.O_NOFOLLOW | os.O_CLOEXEC,
            0o644,
        )
        try:
            st = os.fstat(fd)
            if not stat.S_ISREG(st.st_mode) or st.st_nlink != 1:
                raise DNSError(f"{RUNTIME_RESOLV} is not a private regular file; refusing to use it.")
            os.write(fd, f"# Generated by TTP\n{nameservers}".encode())
            # os.open's mode is filtered by the invoking administrator's umask.
            # This inode becomes /etc/resolv.conf: every resolver client must
            # be able to read it, even though /run/ttp itself stays private.
            os.fchmod(fd, 0o644)
        finally:
            os.close(fd)

        # 2. Symlink check: resolve the real target for mount --bind
        target = RESOLV_CONF
        if os.path.islink(str(RESOLV_CONF)):
            target = Path(os.path.realpath(str(RESOLV_CONF)))

        # 3. Clear any stale mount stacks (idempotency guard)
        _clear_stale_mounts(str(target))

        # 4. Overlay via mount --bind (non-destructive).
        #    mount(8) resolves its source argument itself, in its own process,
        #    so the descriptor above cannot be handed to it: /proc/self/fd/<n>
        #    would name mount's file table, not ours. Instead, re-check by
        #    lstat that the name still denotes the exact inode just written --
        #    same device and inode, still a single-linked regular file -- and
        #    refuse if it does not. /run/ttp is root-owned, so nothing below
        #    root can substitute the entry in the interval this narrows.
        _assert_is(RUNTIME_RESOLV, st)
        subprocess.run(
            [resolve("mount"), "--bind", str(RUNTIME_RESOLV), str(target)],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            check=True,
            timeout=10,
        )

        return {
            "mode": "overlay",
            "mount_target": str(target),
            "systemd_resolved": resolved_active,
        }
    except Exception as e:
        # Clean up any systemd-resolved drop-in if we failed during overlay setup
        if resolved_active:
            try:
                from ttp import dns_resolved

                dns_resolved.restore_resolved()
            except Exception:
                pass

        if isinstance(e, subprocess.CalledProcessError):
            raise DNSError(f"Command failed: {e.cmd} -> {e.stderr.strip()}") from e
        raise DNSError(f"Failed to apply DNS configuration: {e}") from e

def detect_active_interface() -> str:
    """Detect the primary network interface using 'ip route'."""
    try:
        result = subprocess.run(
            [resolve("ip"), "route", "show", "default"],
            capture_output=True,
            text=True,
            check=True,
            timeout=10,
        )
        # Output example: "default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp..."
        parts = result.stdout.split()
        if "dev" in parts:
            return parts[parts.index("dev") + 1]
    except (subprocess.CalledProcessError, IndexError):
        pass
    return "eth0"  # Sane fallback if detection fails

def restore_dns(backup: dict[str, Any] | None) -> None:
    """Restore original system DNS settings by unmounting the overlay.

    If systemd-resolved was active on startup, also removes the volatile
    drop-in configuration and restarts it.
    """
    # The backup comes from the session lock, which is state rather than a
    # trusted structure. A wrong type here used to raise out of do_stop after
    # the firewall was already destroyed, leaving the overlay mounted with no
    # way to clear it through ttp; and a falsy value made this a silent no-op
    # that still reported success. Derive the target instead of trusting it.
    if not isinstance(backup, dict):
        if backup:
            logger.warning("Ignoring malformed DNS backup of type %s", type(backup).__name__)
        backup = {}

    target = RESOLV_CONF
    if os.path.islink(str(RESOLV_CONF)):
        target = Path(os.path.realpath(str(RESOLV_CONF)))

    # 1. Unmount TTP DNS overlay first to restore the base /etc/resolv.conf file
    mount_target = backup.get("mount_target") or str(target)

    if _is_ttp_mount(mount_target):
        try:
            # Lazy unmount ensures immediate release even if busy
            subprocess.run(
                [resolve("umount"), "-l", mount_target],
                capture_output=True,
                text=True,
                check=True,
                timeout=10,
            )
            logger.info("Successfully unmounted DNS overlay on %s", mount_target)
        except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
            err_msg = e.stderr.strip() if e.stderr else str(e)
            logger.warning("Failed to unmount DNS overlay on %s: %s", mount_target, err_msg)
    else:
        logger.debug("DNS target %s is not mounted, skipping unmount", mount_target)

    # 2. Handle systemd-resolved teardown second (so it reads the restored base resolv.conf)
    if backup.get("systemd_resolved"):
        try:
            from ttp import dns_resolved

            dns_resolved.restore_resolved()
        except Exception as e:
            logger.warning("Failed to restore systemd-resolved: %s", e)

    # 3. Cleanup the ephemeral file to free tmpfs space
    try:
        if RUNTIME_RESOLV.exists():
            RUNTIME_RESOLV.unlink()
    except OSError as e:
        logger.debug("Failed to remove runtime resolv.conf: %s", e)

docs.text:
State management - Volatile lock file for crash-safe operations.

This module acts as the "memory" of TTP. It tracks active sessions using a JSON-formatted lock file stored in /run/ttp/ (a tmpfs mount). Because the lock lives on a volatile filesystem, it vanishes on reboot, eliminating stale-lock issues after power loss.

The only persistent path used by TTP is /var/lib/ttp/ which is managed by ttp.ux (one-time UX engagement features).

CORE CONCEPTS: - Lock File: Located at /run/ttp/ttp.lock (volatile - tmpfs). - Orphans: A lock exists but the recorded PID is dead. - Recovery: The process of reading an orphan lock and calling rollback logic.

def attempt_recovery(
    destroy_firewall: Callable[[], Any],
    restore_dns: Callable[[Any], Any],
) -> bool:
    """Attempt automatic recovery from an orphaned lock.

    Reads the lock, invokes the firewall and DNS restoration
    callbacks, then deletes the lock.  Returns ``True`` on success.

    Parameters
    ----------
    destroy_firewall:
        ``firewall.destroy_rules()``
    restore_dns:
        ``dns.restore_dns(backup)``
    """
    data = read_lock()
    if data is None:
        return False

    try:
        destroy_firewall()
        restore_dns(data.get("dns_backup"))
    finally:
        delete_lock()

    return True

def check_tmpfs_space(min_bytes: int = MIN_TMPFS_BYTES) -> None:
    """Abort if ``/run`` (tmpfs) has insufficient free space.

    Must be called **before** any I/O to ``/run`` so that TTP
    fails fast instead of crashing mid-setup with ``ENOSPC``.

    Raises
    ------
    StateError
        If free space on ``/run`` is below *min_bytes*.
    """
    try:
        usage = shutil.disk_usage("/run")
        if usage.free < min_bytes:
            free_mb = usage.free / (1024 * 1024)
            min_mb = min_bytes / (1024 * 1024)
            raise StateError(
                f"Insufficient space on /run (tmpfs): {free_mb:.1f}MB free, "
                f"minimum {min_mb:.1f}MB required. "
                f"Free space before starting TTP."
            )
    except OSError:
        # Cannot stat /run - non-fatal, proceed with best effort. (StateError is
        # not an OSError, so the error raised above is never caught here.)
        pass

Create /run/ttp, owned by root, and the watchdog's own subdirectory.

Must be called early in the CLI startup before any I/O that targets the runtime directory (lock file, log file, torrc, etc.).

The directory itself stays root-owned. Root creates several files in here by fixed name -- the lock, the log, the generated resolv.conf and the nftables ruleset -- and reopens them by path. Handing the directory to ttp-watchdog let that account unlink any of those entries and put a symlink in their place (the directory carries no sticky bit), which redirected a root-privileged create, chmod, write or bind-mount to a file of its choosing. Ownership of the directory is the capability; the individual files' 0600 modes never protected against it.

The watchdog needs two things and gets exactly those: group search/read on this directory so it can read the lock, and its own subdirectory for anything it writes itself.

def ensure_runtime_dir() -> None:
    """Create ``/run/ttp``, owned by root, and the watchdog's own subdirectory.

    Must be called early in the CLI startup before any I/O that targets
    the runtime directory (lock file, log file, torrc, etc.).

    The directory itself stays **root-owned**. Root creates several files in
    here by fixed name -- the lock, the log, the generated ``resolv.conf`` and
    the nftables ruleset -- and reopens them by path. Handing the directory to
    ttp-watchdog let that account unlink any of those entries and put a symlink
    in their place (the directory carries no sticky bit), which redirected a
    root-privileged create, chmod, write or bind-mount to a file of its
    choosing. Ownership of the directory is the capability; the individual
    files' 0600 modes never protected against it.

    The watchdog needs two things and gets exactly those: group search/read on
    this directory so it can read the lock, and its own subdirectory for
    anything it writes itself.
    """
    LOCK_DIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    gid = _watchdog_gid()
    os.chown(LOCK_DIR, 0, gid if gid is not None else 0)
    os.chmod(LOCK_DIR, 0o750 if gid is not None else 0o700)

    if gid is None:
        return

    # Derived from LOCK_DIR rather than the module constant so that callers
    # (and tests) which redirect LOCK_DIR move the whole tree together.
    watchdog_dir = LOCK_DIR / WATCHDOG_DIR.name
    watchdog_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    os.chown(watchdog_dir, _watchdog_uid_or_root(), gid)
    os.chmod(watchdog_dir, 0o700)

def is_orphan() -> bool:
    """Return ``True`` if the lock file exists but its PID is dead or recycled.

    Uses ``os.kill(pid, 0)`` which sends no signal but raises
    ``OSError`` when the target process does not exist.
    """
    data = read_lock()
    if data is None:
        return False

    pid = data.get("pid")
    if pid is None:
        return True  # corrupt lock -> treat as orphan

    try:
        os.kill(pid, 0)
        if not _is_pid_ttp(pid):
            return True  # PID is alive but not TTP -> recycled (orphan)
    except OSError:
        return True  # process not running -> orphan
    return False

def read_lock(*, strict: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    """Read and return the lock data, or ``None`` if no lock exists."""
    try:
        data = json.loads(LOCK_PATH.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        if isinstance(data, dict):
            return data
        if strict:
            raise StateError("Session lock is not an object")
        return None
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return None
    except PermissionError as exc:
        # /run/ttp is root:ttp-watchdog 0750 once any session has run, so a
        # normal user lands here whether or not a session is active. That is
        # not "no session", and not a damaged lock either: say what to do.
        if strict:
            raise StateError(
                f"The session state in {LOCK_DIR} is readable only by root. Run this command with sudo."
            ) from exc
        return None
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, OSError) as exc:
        if strict:
            raise StateError("Cannot read the session intent") from exc
        return None

        return False

    logger.warning(
        "Watchdog: Initiating auto-healing for failed component '%s'...",
        failed_component,
    )
    try:
        if failed_component == "tor":
            logger.info("Watchdog: Restarting Tor service via systemctl...")
            res = subprocess.run(
                [resolve("systemctl"), "restart", "ttp-tor.service"],
                capture_output=True,
                text=True,
                check=False,
                timeout=10,
            )
            if res.returncode == 0:
                logger.info("Watchdog: Restarted Tor service successfully.")
                return True
            else:
                logger.error(
                    "Watchdog: Failed to restart Tor service: %s",
                    res.stderr.strip() if res.stderr else f"Exit code {res.returncode}",
                )
                return False
